title: Why Good Evidence Sometimes Fails to Change Our Minds
author: Science of Learning
summary: Strong evidence alone is often insufficient to change teachers' professional beliefs and instructional practices, and this article examines why. When pedagogical approaches become deeply associated with professional values—inquiry learning with student curiosity and agency, explicit instruction with teacher control—questioning the approach feels like an attack on the underlying value rather than a discussion of evidence. These associations are not accidental: teacher education programs, policy documents, and professional communities often explicitly link particular methods with prized ideals. When beliefs become part of professional identity, changing them requires much more than simply presenting better data. The article draws on conceptual change research to explain how professional learning can be redesigned to acknowledge the emotional dimensions of belief change, separating instructional methods from the values they have come to symbolize. Practically, this means creating conditions where educators can encounter contradictory evidence without feeling that their core commitments are under attack.

quotes: Highlights Strong evidence alone is often not enough to change professional beliefs.
Teachers naturally interpret new evidence through beliefs they already hold.
Instructional approaches often become symbols of educational values like curiosity, equity, or student agency.
When instructional beliefs become part of our professional identity, changing our minds becomes even harder.
Conceptual change research offers practical ways to make professional learning more effective.
One of the enduring puzzles of teacher education is why strong research evidence so often fails to change teachers’ beliefs about instruction.
Most of us like to believe that if we were shown strong evidence contradicting one of our beliefs, we would simply change our minds.
We see ourselves as thoughtful, rational people who are willing to follow the evidence.
